processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Ingots (nominal Fe-35Mn-19Al-5Cu at.%, melted in a vacuum induction furnace under argon) were homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h.
Homogenized ingots were hot-rolled into plates with a thickness of 4 mm.
Samples solution treated at 1100 °C for 10 min under an argon atmosphere, followed by oil quenching (this is the parent process proc_st-1100c-10min-oq).
Solution-treated 19Al samples were aged at 600 °C for 1 h, followed by water quenching.

structures.overall_structure: For the 19Al (Fe-35Mn-19Al-5Cu) alloy aged at 600 °C for 1 h, the α (BCC) matrix had almost completely transformed into β-Mn, leaving a predominantly β-Mn structure with numerous fine precipitates (BCC and FCC Cu-rich phases) distributed within/at the interfaces of the β-Mn.

phases_present.morphology: dominant matrix formed by near-complete α→β-Mn transformation
residual matrix, almost completely transformed into β-Mn after 1 h at 600 °C
new fine precipitates distributed within the β-Mn
fine particles at the interfaces between β-Mn

precipitates.distribution: fine precipitates distributed within the β-Mn

interfaces.phase_evolution: Proposed sequence for Fe-Mn-Al-Cu low-density steels: α → α + FCC Cu-rich phase → α-Mn + β-Mn + BCC phase → β-Mn + BCC phase + FCC Cu-rich phase. For 19Al aged at 600 °C for 1 h, the α matrix had almost completely transformed into β-Mn, i.e. reaching the β-Mn + BCC phase + FCC Cu-rich phase stage.
interfaces.interface_notes: In the ultra-hard alloys new BCC and FCC Cu-rich phases form at the interfaces between the β-Mn. The FCC Cu-rich phase content between β-Mn interfaces decreases with increasing Al content. No specific interface crystallography/coherence data are reported for the 19Al 600 °C/1 h condition.

measurement_conditions.specimen_geometry: 10 × 5 × 2 mm^3 samples for Vickers hardness measurements
measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Vickers hardness measured with a load of 9.8 N for 15 s; each sample tested 5 times and hardness averaged; surfaces electrolytically polished with 10% perchloric acid + 90% ethanol.

characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Load 9.8 N for 15 s; each sample measured 5 times and averaged; samples electrolytically polished (10% perchloric acid + 90% ethanol).
characterization_methods.purpose: Measure the Vickers hardness of the 19Al alloy after aging at 600 °C for 1 h (reported in Table 4).
characterization_methods.key_findings: 19Al aged at 600 °C for 1 h: 901.2 ± 14.6 HV, one of the near-peak values of the 19Al alloy.

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: ZEISS Sigma 300 SEM operated at 5 kV
characterization_methods.purpose: Characterize the precipitation of secondary phases (α-Mn/β-Mn) and new precipitates in the 19Al alloy after different aging treatments (Fig. 9).
characterization_methods.key_findings: The 600 °C - 1 h panel (Fig. 9) shows a matrix labelled β-Mn with arrows to fine features, consistent with the near-complete α→β-Mn transformation.

unmapped_findings: The 19Al alloy (Fe-35Mn-19Al-5Cu at.%) has EDS-measured chemical composition Fe 41.6, Mn 34.8, Al 18.6, Cu 5.0 at.% (Table 1) and an Archimedes density of 6.66 g·cm^-3 (b0012, b0013, b0017).

Increasing Al content slows the β-Mn precipitation kinetics: for the 19Al alloy the α→β-Mn transformation was complete only after 10 h at 550 °C, but at 600 °C and above the α had almost completely transformed into β-Mn after just 1 h of aging (b0053).

The optimal aging temperature range for achieving ultra-high hardness (resolvable from the hardness contour maps) increases with Al content: ~525–600 °C for 15Al, ~550–600 °C for 17Al and ~575–625 °C for 19Al (b0038).

The 19Al solution-treated baseline hardness is 263.8 ± 1.1 HV, and its overall aged hardness window spans 263.8 HV to 917.8 HV (Table 4); the 19Al peak of 917.8 ± 24.5 HV occurred after aging at 600 °C for 10 h, i.e. a different condition from this 600 °C/1 h sample (b0031, b0032).
